issues.legal_issue: A lease permitting residence and a personal office, while prohibiting commercial use, is for residential use only when the personal office is not a place for conducting business.
material_facts: The lease permitted use of the premises for residence and a personal office, and expressly prohibited commercial use.
The premises were described as a house with bedrooms, living areas and other residential facilities; no office room was described or space set aside for an office.
The tenant could use any part of the premises as a personal office, where outsiders would not normally be admitted and commercial transactions would not take place.
The lease required the landlord to pay taxes provided the premises were used for residence only, and the landlord paid those taxes.

The landlord sought eviction on a residential-use ground; the Rent Controller ordered eviction, but the High Court reversed that order on the basis that the permitted office use made the tenancy composite.
issues.conclusion: The lease was for residential use only. The personal-office permission did not make the letting composite or take it outside the residential eviction ground, so the High Court’s order was set aside and the Rent Controller’s eviction order restored.
issues.legal_principle: A document is construed by giving its words their normal and natural meaning, reading the document as a whole rather than piecemeal. The meaning of “office” depends on the language and context, since the word has several meanings; a personal office that is not a place for conducting business may be consistent with residential use. The Court applied Section 14(1)(e) and referred to the definition of premises in Section 2(i) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. It relied on Krishna Biharilal v. Gulabchand, D.D.A. v. D.C. Kaushish, Monypenny v. Monypenny and In re Meredith, ex parte Chick for document construction, and Macmillan v. Guest and Smt. Kanta Kathuria v. Manak Chand Surana on the varied meanings of “office”; D.D.A. v. D.C. Kaushish also referred to Sections 90–94 of the Indian Evidence Act as recognizing the primary rule of construction.

rule.if: residential_rent_eviction_case and lease_allows_residence and lease_permits_only_personal_office and lease_expressly_excludes_commercial_use and personal_office_is_noncommercial_domestic_use and no_office_space_is_separately_earmarked and landlord_bears_taxes_only_during_residential_use

predicates.residential_rent_eviction_case: A landlord brought a rent-control proceeding seeking eviction on the basis that the premises were let for residential use.
predicates.lease_allows_residence: The lease permitted the tenant to use the premises as a residence.
predicates.lease_permits_only_personal_office: The lease allowed the tenant to maintain a personal office, rather than an office for conducting the tenant’s business or official work.
predicates.lease_expressly_excludes_commercial_use: The lease expressly prohibited the tenant from using the premises for commercial purposes.
predicates.personal_office_is_noncommercial_domesti: The permitted personal office was a place where outsiders would not normally be admitted and commercial transactions would not take place.
predicates.no_office_space_is_separately_earmarked: The lease described residential accommodation without identifying an existing office room or allocating separate space for an office.
predicates.landlord_bears_taxes_only_during_residen: The lease placed responsibility for the premises’ taxes on the landlord while the premises were used for residence.

issues.definition: When a residential rent-eviction proceeding concerns a lease that permits residence and only a noncommercial personal office, excludes commercial use, and contains the stated residential features, residential eviction is permissible.
